completeWords.paragraph: Microplastics are fragments smaller than five millim___ (1) that originate from degraded packaging, synthetic fibers, and industrial pellets. Because they are buoy___ (2) or neutrally dense, currents can trans___ (3) them across oceans. Laboratory studies show that some organisms ingest these particles, confusing them with prey, which can reduce feed___ (4) efficiency. Researchers also investigate whether microplastics act as vectors for adsor___ (5) pollutants that later des___ (6) in digestive fluids. However, estimating real-world risk is challenging: field samples can be contami___ (7) during collection, and particle concentrations vary widely by location and depth. To improve comparability, scientists now standardize filtration mesh size and report both particle count and mass-based metri___ (8). Long-term monitoring aims to detect trends and evaluate whether policy bans on microbeads have a measu___ (9) effect. Even so, uncertainty remains about how plastics interact with gut microb___ (10) and immune responses.

Common wrong: millimetres (UK spelling may be marked wrong)

Meaning able to float; explains transport.

Verb fits currents moving particles.

Modifies efficiency; about eating behavior.
Common wrong: feed (wrong form)

Particles can carry adsorbed pollutants on surfaces.
Common wrong: absorbed (different process)

Verb meaning release from a surface; pollutants can desorb.

Field samples can be contaminated; fits method limitation.
Common wrong: contaminant (noun)

notice.label: NOTICE
notice.text: To reduce laboratory contamination, the Coastal Research Lab is moving to a ‘no fleece’ policy. Starting next week, staff and visitors must avoid wearing synthetic-fiber outerwear in the clean sampling room. Cotton lab coats will be provided at the entrance. Samples arriving without sealed lids will be rejected and must be re-collected.

questions.question: Why is the lab introducing the new policy?
choices: To increase the number of visitors
To lower the price of lab coats
To reduce contamination of samples
To encourage fleece manufacturing
questions.explanation:
The notice says the goal is to reduce laboratory contamination.
Why (A) is wrong: Visitors are not being recruited.
Why (B) is wrong: No pricing issue is mentioned.
Why (D) is wrong: It discourages synthetic fibers, not encourages them.

questions.question: What will happen to samples without sealed lids?
choices: They will be stored for later analysis
They will be rejected and need to be collected again
They will be cleaned in the sampling room
They will be mailed back to the sender
questions.explanation:
It explicitly states such samples will be rejected and must be re-collected.
Why (A) is wrong: Storage is not offered as an option.
Why (C) is wrong: Cleaning is not mentioned.
Why (D) is wrong: Mailing back is not stated.

post.label: POST
post.text: @OceanFactsDaily: A reminder that ‘microplastics in fish’ headlines can be misleading. Detection depends on lab methods, and some studies count fibers that may come from clothing. Ask: How were samples collected? What blanks/controls were used?

questions.question: What is the post mainly encouraging readers to do?
choices: Evaluate study methods before accepting headlines
Buy synthetic clothing to test contamination
Assume all detected fibers come from fish
Ignore all research about microplastics
questions.explanation:
It advises questioning methods and not taking headlines at face value.
Why (D) is wrong: It does not say to ignore all research.
Why (C) is wrong: It warns that some fibers may come from clothing contamination.
Why (B) is wrong: It does not promote buying synthetic clothing.

questions.question: Why does the post mention blanks/controls?
choices: To highlight procedures that check for contamination
To argue that newspapers should be banned
To suggest controls make results less accurate
To explain how to feed fish in laboratories
questions.explanation:
Blanks/controls help identify contamination introduced during sampling or analysis.
Why (C) is wrong: Controls improve, not reduce, reliability.
Why (D) is wrong: Feeding fish is unrelated.
Why (B) is wrong: No bans are proposed.

message.label: MESSAGE
message.text: Team—please remember to run a procedural blank with every batch this week. We changed the filter brand, and I want to confirm the background fiber count hasn’t shifted. Log the blank results in the shared sheet before you process real samples.

questions.question: Why does the writer want procedural blanks run this week?
choices: To train new staff on spreadsheet design
To check whether a change in filters affects contamination levels
To speed up sample processing
To replace real samples with blanks
questions.explanation:
They changed the filter brand and want to verify background fiber counts.
Why (C) is wrong: It may slow processing, not speed it up.
Why (D) is wrong: Real samples are still processed after blanks.
Why (A) is wrong: The spreadsheet is for logging, not training on design.

academicPassage.title: Interpreting Microplastic Exposure in Marine Food Webs
academicPassage.passage:
Reports of microplastics in seafood often imply a direct threat to human health, but the scientific picture is more nuanced. First, microplastics vary in polymer type, shape, and size, which affects how organisms encounter and retain them. Some particles pass through digestive systems quickly, while others may lodge in tissues, especially when they are extremely small.

Second, researchers debate whether microplastics meaningfully increase exposure to chemical pollutants. Although plastics can carry pollutants on their surfaces, an organism’s diet already contains many contaminant sources. In some cases, the quantity desorbed from plastics may be minor compared with background exposure. Consequently, laboratory experiments that use unrealistically high particle concentrations may overstate risk.

Finally, measurement itself is difficult. Fibers shed from clothing or airborne dust can contaminate samples unless strict controls are used. For this reason, many scientists emphasize method transparency and replication. Rather than treating any detection as alarming, they argue that policymakers should focus on robust trends—such as whether concentrations are rising in particular regions—and on interventions that reduce plastic release at its source.

questions.question: Why does the author say the scientific picture is ‘more nuanced’?
choices: Because microplastics are harmless in all cases
Because scientists have stopped studying pollution
Because seafood contains no contaminants
Because microplastics differ in properties and their impacts vary
questions.explanation:
The passage lists multiple factors—particle variability, pollutant debate, and measurement challenges—that complicate simple conclusions.
Why (A) is wrong: It does not claim harmlessness.
Why (B) is wrong: Research is ongoing.
Why (C) is wrong: It notes background contaminants exist.

questions.question: What point does the passage make about pollutants carried on plastics?
choices: They may contribute less than background dietary exposure
They cannot desorb in digestive systems
They are always the dominant exposure source
They only matter for large plastic pieces
questions.explanation:
It says desorbed pollutants may be minor compared with existing dietary exposure sources.
Why (C) is wrong: It explicitly questions dominance.
Why (B) is wrong: Desorption is discussed as possible.
Why (D) is wrong: Small particles are emphasized, not only large pieces.

questions.question: Why might some laboratory experiments overstate risk?
choices: They include too many different polymer types
They avoid using strict controls
They use particle concentrations higher than typical real-world levels
They measure plastics only by mass
questions.explanation:
The author notes experiments using unrealistically high concentrations may exaggerate risk.
Why (B) is wrong: Strict controls are recommended, not avoided.
Why (A) is wrong: Polymer variety is not the stated reason.
Why (D) is wrong: Mass-only measurement is not the main critique.

questions.question: In paragraph 3, ‘contaminate’ most nearly means
choices: to preserve by sealing tightly
to make impure by introducing unwanted material
to measure using standardized tools
to reduce by filtering
questions.explanation:
Contaminate means to introduce unwanted fibers or dust that distort results.
Why (A) is wrong: Sealing tightly is the opposite action.
Why (C) is wrong: Measurement standardization is separate.
Why (D) is wrong: Filtering reduces contamination; it is not the meaning.

questions.question: Which approach does the author favor for policy?
choices: Banning seafood consumption
Responding to any detection as a crisis
Limiting research to laboratory studies
Focusing on robust trends and reducing plastic release at the source
questions.explanation:
The final sentence supports trend-focused policy and source reduction rather than alarm over any detection.
Why (B) is wrong: The passage rejects treating any detection as automatically alarming.
Why (A) is wrong: No seafood ban is suggested.
Why (C) is wrong: It calls for transparency and replication, not lab-only limits.

completeWords.paragraph: Archaeologists rarely rely on a single test; instead, they build an evid___ (1) chain from stratigraphy, artifacts, and absolute dating. Radiocarbon dating estimates age by measuring the decay of carbon-14, but results must be cali___ (2) using known atmospheric variations. Samples can yield misleading dates if they are contami___ (3) with modern carbon or if older material is redepo___ (4) into newer layers. For this reason, researchers prefer short-lived materials such as seeds, which reduce the ‘old wood’ eff___ (5). They also compare multiple samples and report a confidence interv___ (6) rather than a single point estimate. Beyond radiocarbon, thermoluminescence dating can be applied to heated minerals, and obsidian hydration can provide relative chron___ (7) when local rates are known. In all cases, interpretation depends on site context and on documenting the prove___ (8) of each specimen. When evidence sources converge, conclusions become more rob___ (9); when they diverge, archaeologists revise hypotheses or collect addit___ (10) data.
explanations:
Fits ‘evidence chain’ phrase.
Common wrong: evident (adj)

Radiocarbon dates are calibrated; standard term.
Common wrong: calculated (too general)

Modern carbon contamination is common issue.
Common wrong: contaminate (verb form)

Older material moved into newer layers.
Common wrong: reposted (wrong)

‘Old wood effect’ is standard phrasing.
Common wrong: affect (wrong usage)

Confidence interval is statistical range.
Common wrong: interview (wrong)

Relative chronology is timeline ordering.
Common wrong: chronicle (wrong nuance)

Origin/context of artifact; crucial in archaeology.
Common wrong: province (different word)

Means strong/reliable; used in research claims.
Common wrong: robot (spelling)

More data; fits ‘collect additional data’.
Common wrong: addictive (wrong)

notice.label: NOTICE
notice.text: Field School Participants: All soil samples must be labeled with trench number, depth, and date before leaving the site. Unlabeled bags cannot be processed in the lab because their stratigraphic context is unverifiable. If you make an error, cross it out with a single line and rewrite—do not use correction fluid. Submit your sample log at the end of each day.

questions.question: Why can’t unlabeled soil samples be processed?
choices: They are illegal to collect
They will damage lab equipment
Their stratigraphic context cannot be verified
They are too heavy to transport
questions.explanation:
The notice says context is unverifiable without labels, so the lab cannot process them.
Why (D) is wrong: Weight is not mentioned.
Why (B) is wrong: Equipment damage is not stated.
Why (A) is wrong: Collection legality is not discussed.

questions.question: What should participants do if they make a labeling error?
choices: Use correction fluid to erase it
Leave it blank and explain later
Throw away the sample
Cross it out and rewrite it
questions.explanation:
It instructs participants to cross out with a single line and rewrite, and not to use correction fluid.
Why (C) is wrong: Discarding is not recommended.
Why (A) is wrong: Correction fluid is explicitly forbidden.
Why (B) is wrong: Leaving blank is not allowed.

post.label: POST
post.text: @MuseumBehindScenes: Today we rejected a ‘rare’ pot offered by a seller because the paperwork didn’t show where it was excavated. Without provenance, an object tells us almost nothing about past behavior—and it might be stolen. Context matters more than rarity.

questions.question: What is the main message of the post?
choices: Rare objects are always authentic
Provenance is essential for scientific and ethical reasons
Museums should buy artifacts quickly
Paperwork is less important than appearance
questions.explanation:
It emphasizes that without provenance, objects lose scientific value and may be unethical to acquire.
Why (A) is wrong: It does not guarantee authenticity.
Why (C) is wrong: It argues against buying without context.
Why (D) is wrong: It says context matters more than rarity.

questions.question: Why might a museum reject an artifact without provenance?
choices: It provides little information and could be stolen
It always comes from a modern factory
It cannot be dated with radiocarbon methods
It is too fragile to display
questions.explanation:
The post states it tells little about past behavior and might be stolen.
Why (C) is wrong: Radiocarbon is not the sole reason for rejection.
Why (D) is wrong: Fragility is not mentioned.
Why (B) is wrong: It does not claim all such objects are modern.

message.label: MESSAGE
message.text: Dr. Patel—our charcoal samples from Layer IV produced dates older than the pottery style suggests. Could bioturbation have mixed material upward, or should we suspect redeposition during flooding? I’m attaching the stratigraphy photos for your thoughts.

questions.question: Why is the writer contacting Dr. Patel?
choices: To ask for an explanation for conflicting dating evidence
To complain about pottery styles
To announce that the site is closed
To request funding for a museum purchase
questions.explanation:
They have conflicting dates and want help interpreting possible causes like mixing or redeposition.
Why (D) is wrong: Funding is not mentioned.
Why (C) is wrong: No closure is announced.
Why (B) is wrong: They are analyzing evidence, not complaining.

academicPassage.title: Why ‘Context’ Is a Form of Data
academicPassage.passage:
In archaeology, an artifact’s scientific value depends heavily on where it is found. A stone tool recovered from a sealed layer alongside animal bones and hearth ash can support inferences about diet and technology. The same tool, purchased from an unknown source, may be aesthetically interesting but scientifically opaque.

This distinction matters because archaeological claims are rarely built on a single object. Researchers instead assemble evidence chains: stratigraphic relationships indicate relative order, while absolute dating methods estimate calendar age. Each link, however, can be weakened. Flooding can redeposit older material into younger sediments; burrowing animals can move objects across layers; and samples can be contaminated during collection. Therefore, archaeologists prefer multiple, independent measurements and detailed recording protocols.

Some critics argue that strict standards slow discovery, but proponents respond that speed is not the central aim. Without documentation, spectacular finds cannot be evaluated or replicated, and they may encourage looting by creating markets for unprovenanced objects. From this perspective, protecting context is not bureaucracy; it is how the discipline converts objects into knowledge.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about an artifact bought from an unknown source?
choices: It can be dated more accurately than excavated artifacts
It is always fake
It has greater value because it is rare
It may be interesting but provides little scientific information
questions.explanation:
The passage contrasts excavated vs unknown-source artifacts, saying the latter is scientifically opaque.
Why (B) is wrong: It does not claim it is always fake.
Why (C) is wrong: Rarity is not equated with scientific value.
Why (A) is wrong: Unknown context does not increase dating accuracy.

questions.question: Why does the author mention flooding and burrowing animals?
choices: To show that stratigraphic context can be disturbed
To explain how to create markets for artifacts
To suggest archaeology should focus on aesthetics
To argue that absolute dating is unnecessary
questions.explanation:
These examples illustrate processes that can mix or move materials, weakening context.
Why (D) is wrong: Absolute dating is still used; the point is limitations.
Why (B) is wrong: Markets are mentioned later, not as the purpose here.
Why (C) is wrong: Aesthetics is contrasted with scientific inference.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, ‘independent’ measurements are recommended mainly to
choices: replace stratigraphy with radiocarbon dating
reduce reliance on any single potentially flawed link in the evidence chain
make reports longer
avoid recording protocols
questions.explanation:
Multiple independent measures protect against error if one link (e.g., contamination) is compromised.
Why (C) is wrong: Length is irrelevant.
Why (A) is wrong: It argues for combining methods, not replacing stratigraphy.
Why (D) is wrong: Recording protocols are emphasized, not avoided.

questions.question: What is the likely position of proponents mentioned in paragraph 3?
choices: They want to ban all absolute dating methods
They think documentation is essential for evaluation and to discourage looting
They oppose any museum displays
They believe speed matters more than documentation
questions.explanation:
Proponents argue documentation is needed for evaluation/replication and to reduce looting incentives.
Why (D) is wrong: They explicitly reject speed as central aim.
Why (C) is wrong: They do not oppose displays; they oppose undocumented acquisition.
Why (A) is wrong: No ban on absolute dating is suggested.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: Flooding is the main cause of dating errors
Radiocarbon dating is the only trustworthy method
Context and documentation are crucial because they turn artifacts into reliable evidence
Archaeology is primarily about buying rare objects
questions.explanation:
Across paragraphs, the passage argues context/documentation make evidence reliable and ethically sourced.
Why (D) is wrong: Buying is portrayed as scientifically weak.
Why (A) is wrong: Flooding is one example, not main focus.
Why (B) is wrong: Radiocarbon is not the only method discussed.
